**Answer: Yes.**

**Proof.** Let $f_n \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous with $f_n \to f$ pointwise, and write $f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)$. Fix an arbitrary constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. We prove that $\{x : f(x) \ge c\}$ is a $G_\delta$ set by showing its complement $\{x : f(x) < c\}$ is an $F_\sigma$ set.

**Claim.**
$$\{x : f(x) < c\} \;=\; \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}\,\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\,\bigcap_{n=N}^{\infty}\,\bigl\{x : f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}\bigr\}.$$

Since each $f_n$ is continuous, every set $\{x : f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}\}$ is **closed**. A countable intersection of closed sets is closed, so each $\bigcap_{n=N}^{\infty}\{f_n \le c-\tfrac{1}{k}\}$ is closed. The right-hand side is therefore a countable union of closed sets, i.e. an $F_\sigma$ set.

**Verification of the claim.**

*($\subseteq$)* Suppose $f(x) < c$. Set $\delta = c - f(x) > 0$ and choose $k$ with $\tfrac{1}{k} < \delta$. Then $f(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$. Since $f_n(x) \to f(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$, there exists $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $f_n(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$, hence $f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}$. Thus $x$ belongs to the right-hand side.

*($\supseteq$)* Suppose $x$ belongs to the right-hand side. Then for some $k$ and some $N$, we have $f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}$ for every $n \ge N$. Taking the limit,
$$f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k} < c.$$
Hence $f(x) < c$, so $x \in \{f < c\}$.

The two inclusions establish the claim, so $\{x : f(x) < c\}$ is $F_\sigma$.

**Conclusion.** Its complement
$$\{x : f(x) \ge c\} \;=\; \mathbb{R} \setminus \{x : f(x) < c\}$$
is the complement of an $F_\sigma$ set, hence a $G_\delta$ set. Since $c \in \mathbb{R}$ was arbitrary, the pointwise convergence of continuous functions guarantees that for **every** constant $c$, the set $\{x : f(x) \ge c\}$ is a $G_\delta$ set. $\blacksquare$

**Proof.** Let $f_n \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous with $f_n \to f$ pointwise, and write $f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)$. Fix an arbitrary constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. We prove that $\{x : f(x) \ge c\}$ is a $G_\delta$ set by showing its complement $\{x : f(x) < c\}$ is an $F_\sigma$ set.

**Claim.**
$$\{x : f(x) < c\} \;=\; \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}\,\bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty}\,\bigcap_{n=N}^{\infty}\,\bigl\{x : f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}\bigr\}.$$

Since each $f_n$ is continuous, every set $\{x : f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}\}$ is **closed**. A countable intersection of closed sets is closed, so each $\bigcap_{n=N}^{\infty}\{f_n \le c-\tfrac{1}{k}\}$ is closed. The right-hand side is therefore a countable union of closed sets, i.e. an $F_\sigma$ set.

**Verification of the claim.**

*($\subseteq$)* Suppose $f(x) < c$. Set $\delta = c - f(x) > 0$ and choose $k$ with $\tfrac{1}{k} < \delta$. Then $f(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$. Since $f_n(x) \to f(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$, there exists $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $f_n(x) < c - \tfrac{1}{k}$, hence $f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}$. Thus $x$ belongs to the right-hand side.

*($\supseteq$)* Suppose $x$ belongs to the right-hand side. Then for some $k$ and some $N$, we have $f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k}$ for every $n \ge N$. Taking the limit,
$$f(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x) \le c - \tfrac{1}{k} < c.$$
Hence $f(x) < c$, so $x \in \{f < c\}$.

The two inclusions establish the claim, so $\{x : f(x) < c\}$ is $F_\sigma$.

**Conclusion.** Its complement
$$\{x : f(x) \ge c\} \;=\; \mathbb{R} \setminus \{x : f(x) < c\}$$
is the complement of an $F_\sigma$ set, hence a $G_\delta$ set. Since $c \in \mathbb{R}$ was arbitrary, the pointwise convergence of continuous functions guarantees that for **every** constant $c$, the set $\{x : f(x) \ge c\}$ is a $G_\delta$ set. $\blacksquare$
